Question: Two subsets of the set \(S = \{a, b, c, d, e\}\) are to be chosen so that their union is \(S\) and their intersection contains exactly two elements. In how many ways can this be done, assuming that the order in which the subsets are chosen does not matter?
Solution:
Method 1: Choose the intersection, then split the rest

First choose the two elements that belong to both subsets. There are
\[
\binom52=\frac{5\cdot4}{2}=10
\]
choices: choosing them in sequence counts each pair twice.

Each of the other three elements must belong to exactly one subset. Belonging to neither would violate the union condition, and belonging to both would enlarge the intersection. Because the subsets are unordered, their exclusive elements can split in just two ways:

If all three go together, one subset is the chosen intersection and the other is \(S\). This gives one pair.

If they split as one element and two elements, choosing the lone element determines the pair. This gives three pairs. There is no duplication because the subset receiving the lone element is uniquely distinguished by its smaller size.

These cases exhaust all splits of three elements. Also, every valid pair has a unique intersection, so different intersection choices cannot overlap. The total is
\[
10(1+3)=\boxed{40},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).

Method 2: Count labeled subsets, then remove the labels

Temporarily label the two subsets \(A\) and \(B\). Choose their two common elements in \(\binom52=10\) ways. Every remaining element must go into exactly one of \(A\) and \(B\), giving two choices for each of three elements. Thus the number of labeled pairs is
\[
10\cdot2^3=80.
\]
This construction includes every valid labeled pair exactly once: its intersection specifies the first choice, and membership of the remaining elements specifies the three assignments.

Now remove the labels. The subsets cannot be equal, since equal subsets would have the same union and intersection, whereas those sizes here are \(5\) and \(2\). Therefore, every unordered pair has exactly two labeled versions, \((A,B)\) and \((B,A)\). Dividing by this multiplicity gives
\[
\frac{80}{2}=\boxed{40},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).
